title: Indian Students in the US Fall 6.5% as Postgraduate Enrolments Drop by a Third
excerpt: Open Doors 2026 counts 339,435 Indian students — the first decline in five years — with graduate numbers down 34% even as OPT participation hits a record 182,201.
body:
• Indian students in the US fell 6.5% to 339,435 in 2025-26, the first annual decline in five years, according to the Open Doors 2026 report released Monday — though India remained the largest sender for a third straight year.
  • The drop was driven by postgraduate study: Indian graduate enrolments plunged 34% to 116,609, while undergraduate numbers slipped just 1% to 39,711.
  • Indians already in the US are staying to work: participation in Optional Practical Training (OPT) rose 27% to 182,201.
  • For students planning a 2027 start, the early signal is weaker still — a fall 2026 snapshot of more than 800 colleges found graduate enrolments down a further 15%, and nearly 9 in 10 colleges said the visa process is hurting enrolment.

India sent fewer students to the United States in 2025-26 than the year before, ending a run of growth that had made it the largest source of international students on American campuses. The Open Doors 2026 Report on International Educational Exchange, released Monday by the Institute of International Education (IIE) with the US Department of State, counted 339,435 Indian students at US colleges and universities — a 6.5% decline from 363,019 in 2024-25, and the first annual fall since 2020-21.

The headline number understates where the change is happening. Open Doors counts everyone enrolled plus graduates working on Optional Practical Training, and those two groups moved in opposite directions. Indian graduate enrolments — historically the core of the flow, dominated by master's degrees in engineering, technology and management — fell 34%, from 177,892 to 116,609. Undergraduate enrolments were nearly flat, down 1% to 39,711. OPT participation, meanwhile, rose 27% to 182,201, as earlier cohorts of Indian graduates stayed on to work. In other words, the pipeline of students already in the US is still delivering workers; it is the intake of new postgraduates that has contracted.

"The 2026 Open Doors data reaffirms the enduring importance of international education to the United States."

— Jason Czyz, President and CEO, Institute of International Education

A wider retreat, led by master's degrees

India's decline mirrors the overall picture. Total international enrolment fell 3% to 1,146,163, according to the IIE release. New international students — those attending their institution for the first time — dropped 18% to 228,123. Across all countries, master's enrolments fell 22.4% to 237,655, while doctoral numbers rose 3.1% to 158,152 and undergraduate enrolments held roughly steady at 356,165, down 0.3%. China, the second-largest sender, fell 4% to 254,458 students. International students contributed nearly $56 billion to the US economy in 2025, according to the US Department of Commerce figures cited in the release, and made up 6% of the total US higher education population; 57% studied STEM fields.

What the fall snapshot says about 2026-27

Alongside the annual census, IIE published a Fall 2026 Snapshot drawn from more than 800 institutions, offering a preliminary read on the current academic year. It points the same way: international student totals down 9% this fall, new enrolments down 15%, graduate students down 15%, undergraduates down 3% and OPT participation down 6% — the first sign that the OPT cushion may also start to thin as smaller graduate cohorts feed through.

Colleges surveyed put the causes plainly. Nearly 9 out of 10 said the visa process has hurt foreign enrolment, 70% blamed travel restrictions, and 60% cited competition from other countries, according to Higher Ed Dive's report on the survey. "There are more countries actively investing in and recruiting international students," Mirka Martel, IIE's head of research, evaluation and learning, said during a press call. "As a result, this often means that there are more destination opportunities." The report also noted that the Department of Homeland Security has proposed up to $100,000 in new fees for each international student a college recommends for OPT — a proposal colleges have told the administration they cannot afford.

What this means if you are applying

For an Indian family weighing a US master's degree for 2027, the data cuts two ways. Fewer applicants means less competition for seats at many programmes; it also means the binding constraint has shifted from admission to the visa and work-authorisation process that follows it. The students already in the system are still converting study into work — Indian OPT participation is at a record level in this report — but the fall snapshot suggests that route is now narrowing at the entry point. The full dataset is published by IIE at Open Doors Data, and Higher Ed Dive's breakdown of the release details the survey responses behind the fall snapshot.

What to watch next is whether the fall snapshot's declines harden into the 2026-27 census, and whether the proposed OPT fee moves from proposal to rule. Both will shape the decision for the next cohort more than any single university's recruitment pitch.
